newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - U.S. debt futures seen loafing in ranges.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - U.S. debt futures seen loafing in ranges.

text.p: U.S. debt futures are unlikely to make much headway over the next couple of trading days and could loaf inside familiar ranges, chartists and brokers said.
After stalling at 108-07/32, last week's peak, June Treasury bond futures before midday Monday briefly probed below support at 107-28/32 - 27/32 in very quiet trade.
"There's nothing really to write about," said one Treasury bond futures floor broker about the midmorning erosion. "We're maybe just backing up a little before the auctions."
U.S. Treasury will sell two- and five-year notes starting Tuesday, with little other key economic data on tap this week.
Another floor broker Monday called scanty early turnover in June Treasury bond futures a "snoozer-fest."
"I think it has potential to be that way (quiet) here for the entire week," John Nyhoff, chief economist, Tokyo-Mitsubishi Futures (USA) Inc, said of Eurodollar futures.
Noting the sparse data lineup until next Tuesday's March durable goods orders, he added: "It's kind of an 'Oh-my-god-what-are-we-going-to-do-this week?' kind of trade."
In the next two to three weeks, June bonds will follow a technical consolidation pattern in a bear market, said Joseph Plauche, financial futures analyst, Dean Witter Reynolds.
Plauche said June T-bonds, which hit a low April 11 at 106-12/32, have nearly finished an Elliott Wave "a" move back up to 108-12/32.
In the "b" wave, which he said could be completed this week, the contract should retrench back down to 107-04/32, before returning higher again in the "c" wave.
"We made an intermediate bottom (April 11) in a bear market that's not over," Plauche added.
But the fundamental picture turned fuzzy after a tame consumer price index and two weeks of higher jobless claims softened the case for two more Fed tightenings by autumn.
Plauche said June T-bonds and September Eurodollars at their April 11 lows of 106-12/32 and 93.635, respectively, had priced in two more Fed rate hikes by autumn.
"Since that time (April 11), we've received some evidence that's reopened the (tightening) debate," he said. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750)) E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
